doc.title: Adrian Cunningham interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 31, 2021

title: Being an entertainer
summary: He says connecting with the audience matters, finds relief as a sideman, and cites Ellington and Dizzy as entertainers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you ever look out in clubs and, I do this myself if I’m playing in a band and if I look out and if I see people leaning over to each other and yelling at each other that maybe we need to adjust our volume. But that leads me to another sort of inquiry about the role of entertainment in this music, and how it can differ from one setting to another, and are you comfortable with being an entertainer?

Yes and no. I think it’s necessary. I certainly feel a great deal of relief often, being a sideman in someone else’s band because then I can just be — okay now I can just play I don’t have to think about anything else. You know being a band leader is really juggling. You have to do all these things. While you’re playing you have to be thinking about the next tune, or you have to be thinking about, you know, okay who are we going to feature, has everyone been featured, you know there’s just so many things to put together beyond the entertaining thing. But I think it’s really important to connect with your audience and I think it’s something that a lot of musicians perhaps don’t emphasize enough. Because we tend to idolize the great player, you know like Brecker for example. I mean his musicianship is otherworldly that there’s not even a need to talk. But however, we’re not

all Brecker. We’re not all, you know, but you also, I’m hugely influenced also by the history of music, bands like Dizzy or look at Duke Ellington, and they were entertainers. They brought something beyond the music. Duke Ellington’s sets were incredible, and his musicianship, and even the choreography with the horn sections on those early bands. I mean try and get a modern horn section to dance around, they’ll murder you. Are you kidding? They’ll quit on the spot.
People breaking their embochures, clack the trumpets together. Yeah. You want me to what?
